content.title: Singular vs. Plural Noun Forms and Noun-Number Agreement
content.overview: This lesson focuses on ensuring that nouns match the quantity indicated by their preceding modifiers (quantifiers). You will learn to identify singular, plural, and uncountable nouns and pair them correctly with words like 'each,' 'several,' and 'many.'
learning_objectives: Identify quantifiers that dictate whether a noun must be singular or plural.
Recognize and apply correct irregular plural forms.
Distinguish between countable and uncountable nouns to avoid incorrect pluralization.
Ensure noun-number agreement within a phrase.

sections.title: Quantifier-to-Noun Matching
sections.content: A quantifier is a word or phrase (like 'many,' 'each,' or 'three') that indicates the number or amount of a noun. In English, the quantifier must agree with the noun's number. Singular quantifiers include 'a,' 'an,' 'one,' 'each,' and 'every.' These must be followed by a singular noun (e.g., 'each student'). Plural quantifiers include 'several,' 'many,' 'few,' 'both,' and specific numbers greater than one. These must be followed by a plural noun (e.g., 'several students').

sections.title: Irregular Plurals and Uncountable Nouns
sections.content: Not all nouns become plural by adding '-s' or '-es.' Irregular plurals change form entirely (e.g., 'child' becomes 'children,' 'criterion' becomes 'criteria,' 'datum' becomes 'data'). Additionally, uncountable (non-count) nouns represent concepts or masses that cannot be counted individually, such as 'equipment,' 'information,' 'advice,' and 'furniture.' These nouns should not be pluralized with an '-s' even if they refer to multiple items.

sections.title: The Recognition Procedure
sections.content: To solve these questions on the ACT: 1. Locate the noun in the underlined portion. 2. Look immediately to the left for a quantifier or number-word. 3. Determine if that quantifier requires a singular or plural form. 4. Verify if the noun is regular, irregular, or uncountable to ensure the spelling is correct.

worked_examples.question: The biology lab received several specimen for the comparative study. Choose the best revision: A. NO CHANGE; B. specimen's; C. specimens; D. specimenes.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the quantifier. The word 'several' modifies the noun. Step 2: Determine the required number. 'Several' implies more than one, so a plural noun is required. Step 3: Form the plural. The plural of 'specimen' is 'specimens.' Step 4: Evaluate choices. Choice C provides the correct plural form. Choice B is a possessive, and Choice D is a misspelling. Correct answer: C.

worked_examples.question: Each members of the committee had to submit a report by Friday. Choose the best revision: A. NO CHANGE; B. member; C. member's; D. of the member.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the quantifier. The word 'Each' modifies the noun. Step 2: Determine the required number. 'Each' and 'every' always require a singular noun. Step 3: Evaluate choices. 'Members' is plural, so A is wrong. Choice B, 'member,' is the singular form. Choice C is possessive and unnecessary. Correct answer: B.

common_mistakes: Treating 'each' or 'every' as plural because they refer to a group; they always require a singular noun.
Adding '-s' to uncountable nouns like 'equipments' or 'informations.'
Confusing plural forms with possessive forms (adding an apostrophe where only a plural '-s' is needed).
Using the singular form after a specific number greater than one (e.g., 'three apple' instead of 'three apples').
exam_tips: When you see a number or quantity word, immediately check the noun that follows it for agreement.
Watch out for 'data' and 'media'; these are plural forms. The singular forms are 'datum' and 'medium.'
If a noun sounds strange with an '-s' (like 'furnitures'), it is likely an uncountable noun and should stay singular.
content.recap: Noun-number agreement requires matching the noun's form to its quantifier. Use singular nouns for 'each,' 'every,' and 'one.' Use plural nouns for 'many,' 'several,' and 'few.' Be careful with irregular plurals and never pluralize uncountable nouns.

knowledge_claims.content: The quantifiers 'each' and 'every' must always be followed by a singular noun.
Quantifiers such as 'several,' 'many,' 'few,' and 'both' require the noun to be in its plural form.
Uncountable (non-count) nouns, such as 'equipment' and 'information,' do not take a plural '-s' even when referring to multiple items.
Irregular plural nouns like 'children,' 'criteria,' and 'data' do not follow the standard '-s' or '-es' ending rules.
To check for noun-number agreement, identify the quantifier modifying the noun and verify if the noun's form (singular or plural) matches that quantifier's requirement.
It is a common error to use a possessive apostrophe (e.g., 'specimen's') when the context only requires a simple plural form (e.g., 'specimens').
The word 'data' is technically the plural form of 'datum,' though it is often tested for its plural requirement in formal usage.
Unlike 'many,' which is used for countable plural nouns, 'much' is used for uncountable singular masses.
After selecting an answer, reread the quantifier and noun together to ensure they sound natural and follow the singular/plural rules.
Specific numbers greater than one (two, ten, one hundred) must be paired with plural noun forms.
The quantifier 'one' is a singular determiner and must be paired with a singular noun.
Avoid pluralizing nouns that represent abstract concepts or collective masses that cannot be counted, such as 'advice' or 'furniture.'

Which choice uses number consistently?
A) The two analysis produced similar conclusion.
B) The two analyses produced a similar conclusions.

videoLesson.title: Match Noun Number to Quantifier
videoLesson.description: You will recognize noun-and-quantifier pairs and incorrect plural forms in phrases. Use quantifier cues to choose singular, irregular plural, or uncountable noun forms.
